Female Brahmaputra barbel (Ptychobarbus dipogon) attain a maximum standard length of 64.4 centimeters [Li = 64.4 centimeters], a size that reflects the species’ late-maturing life-history strategy in the cold, high-altitude rivers of the Yarlung Tsangpo drainage. This ultimate length substantially exceeds that of many other schizothoracine cyprinids, likely an adaptation to the low productivity and extended growing seasons typical of Himalayan torrent systems. The wet weight of newly emerged larvae, calculated from the mean egg diameter of 3.63 millimeters, is estimated at approximately 0.025 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.025 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the minute size of the yolk-sac fry at the moment of chorion rupture. Following eclosion, these tiny prolarvae remain entirely dependent on their endogenous yolk reserves, undergoing a brief lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Reproductive maturation in female Brahmaputra barbel occurs at a standard length of 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters], a threshold that marks the initiation of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. This size at puberty is notably larger than the corresponding value recorded for males of the species. Males attain sexual maturity at a slightly smaller body size, reaching puberty at a standard length of 35.4 centimeters [Lp = 35.4 centimeters], a difference that is consistent with the general pattern of sexual size dimorphism observed in many cyprinids. The onset of gametogenesis in both sexes is tightly coupled to the seasonal thermal regime, with gonadal development accelerating markedly as water temperatures rise during the spring pre-monsoon period. Field surveys indicate that first spawning typically occurs once individuals have surpassed these critical length thresholds, ensuring sufficient somatic capital to support the energetic demands of egg and milt production.

At a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum lifespan of Brahmaputra barbel reaches approximately 44 years [am = approximately 44 years], making this one of the longest-lived cyprinids known. The maximum body mass achieved by adult individuals is approximately 2,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,200 grams], a substantial weight that positions this species as one of the larger members of the genus Ptychobarbus, attained only after many years of slow, steady growth under the cold thermal conditions prevailing in its native habitat. This remarkable longevity is accompanied by a correspondingly extended reproductive lifespan, allowing females to produce multiple clutches over several decades. The species’ slow somatic growth and delayed maturity are classic hallmarks of a K-selected life-history strategy, shaped by the stable but resource-limited environment of deep, oligotrophic alpine rivers.

In females, attainment of puberty—defined by the onset of gonadal activity—occurs at approximately 13 years after hatching [tp = approximately 13 years after hatching] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extraordinarily late age at sexual maturity is among the highest recorded for any freshwater teleost and reflects the metabolically constrained growth rates characteristic of cold stenothermal fishes. Young females invest heavily in somatic growth during their first decade of life, accumulating the body size necessary to accommodate large, yolk-laden oocytes. The corresponding value for males is slightly later, with puberty reached at approximately 13.5 years after hatching [tp = approximately 13.5 years after hatching] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This minor sex-based disparity in maturation timing may be related to differences in energy allocation between the sexes, with males requiring additional time to develop the gonadal mass necessary for successful sperm competition.

Spawning adults of Ptychobarbus dipogon are iteroparous, typically migrating short distances upstream over gravel-cobble substrates to deposit their demersal, adhesive eggs during the early summer flood pulse. The newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, weighing only 0.025 grams [Wwb = 0.025 grams] at emergence, drift downstream into slower lateral habitats where zooplankton abundance is highest. The delayed maturation and protracted lifespan of this species, with a maximum longevity of approximately 44 years [am = approximately 44 years] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], impose an extreme vulnerability to any increase in adult mortality rates, as the reproductive contribution of older, more fecund females will be disproportionately lost. Conservation efforts must therefore consider the severe demographic consequences of gillnet fisheries that preferentially remove the largest individuals.
